To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) The predatory nature of the Liberian and Sierra Leonean conflicts has been exacerbated by the "resource curse" syndrome; (2) Predatory warlords have used the proceeds from plunder and pillaging to purchase arms, to finance their military campaigns, and to buy the loyalty of their mercenary soldiers and their civilian supporters; (3) In the absence of effective and legitimate governance, predatory warlords have been able to exploit the "resource curse syndrome" to perpetuate their military campaigns
the "resource curse" is the primary factor that has engendered the political instability and economic violence in Liberia, Sierra Leone and Angola.

the "resource curse," the "warlordism syndrome" and the "predatory state syndrome" are three major factors that are associated with the economic violence and the political instability in the war-torn Sub-Saharan African countries.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: (a) Why do armed conflicts and economic violence persist in the post-civil war era? (b) How does economic violence contribute to the perpetuation and exacerbation of armed conflicts? and (c) What can be done to reduce the likelihood of future conflicts and economic violence in modern Africa?

the political economy of predation-induced wars in modern Africa is not only an issue of political violence and economic pillaging, but it is also an issue of the political economy of predatory wars and economic plundering in the post-civil war era of Africa.
the political economy of armed conflicts and the "resource curse" in modern Africa have created conditions that have undermined the prospects of peace and prosperity in the sub-region.
the political economy of armed conflicts and economic violence in modern Africa is a multidimensional phenomenon.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the political economy of armed conflicts and the economic violence in modern Africa have been a source of political instability and humanitarian disasters in the region.
economic violence and predation-induced armed conflict have become the new normal in the post-colo war era of Africa.

armed conflicts have undermined state capabilities, weakened the financial resources of non-governmental organizations, and raised provocative questions about political will and sustaining capacity of the international community to keep the peace.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the international community must be prepared to deal with the "resource curse" and the "predator's paradox" in order to prevent and to contain the spread of armed conflict and economic violence in modern African states.
the "resource curse" is not a new problem.
